rows.defining: Practical technical help requests about specific programming, software or engineering problems, written tersely and informally by users seeking a direct answer

Templated one-line prompts requesting a fixed list of growing conditions (temperature, hydrometry, sunshine, rainfall, humidity, soil type) for a named plant's seed, with the constraint 'in bullets 2 words answer in number'; only the plant name changes.

These are programmatic, task-oriented prompts: instructions wrapped around supplied data (context passages, example lists, label sets, API specs) with strict output constraints, rather than natural conversational chatbot messages.

A grab-bag of real, unrelated, casual, one-shot user prompts to a general-purpose chatbot, with no shared topic or template; the defining trait is their heterogeneity as organically sampled, informal, single-turn user queries (including a jailbreak attempt and a meme-like fragment) rather than any common task or format.

The messages are raw, unpolished user inputs with the instruction and source material combined in one block, often truncated mid-sentence and sometimes carrying scraping artefacts, on varied creative or text-processing tasks. They look like samples from a real-world chat log dataset rather than typical standalone chatbot prompts.
Repeated templated prompt asking the model to judge whether a summary is factually consistent with a truncated news document, answering Yes/No

Unrelated, standalone, real-world information-seeking questions from different users on disparate everyday or practical topics, written casually and briefly, which together look like a random sample of typical general-purpose chatbot queries rather than sharing any template, persona, or special feature.

They are a thematically unrelated mix of standalone, single-turn user prompts that appear to be scraped from real chatbot logs, many with anonymization artefacts (NAME_1) and rough or non-native phrasing, rather than any one shared task or topic.

A grab-bag of unrelated, self-contained, single-turn real-world user prompts on practical/technical topics, with no shared template or persona; the common thread is that they are ordinary, informally-written one-shot information or text-editing requests, some with dataset artefacts like NAME_1 or truncation.

Raw, unrelated one-off user prompts to a general chatbot (likely from a public chat log dataset), featuring anonymisation placeholders like NAME_1, truncation, and non-native or typo-ridden phrasing, rather than a single coherent task or topic.

Short, context-free, terse developer/IT help requests, as if typed quickly into a search box, asking for code, a script, or a fix for a technical error or config problem, with rough grammar and no pleasantries or background.

Prompts contain de-identification placeholders (NAME_1, NAME_2, etc.) and are frequently truncated mid-text, indicating scrubbed and clipped real-world dataset inputs wrapped around pasted news/legal passages.

Prompts with explicit, rigid output specifications or in-prompt few-shot/pseudo-code templates that the model is meant to continue or conform to, typically as raw, truncated, dataset-style user inputs with placeholders such as NAME_1.
Every message has person names replaced by anonymization placeholders (NAME_1, NAME_2, etc.), a dataset artefact that is rare in ordinary chatbot messages.

A grab-bag of heterogeneous, standalone user prompts to an LLM, many of which define or override the model's behavior (persona, mode, output format, or tool-call convention) in the prompt itself, rather than just asking a plain question.

They are a grab-bag of unrelated, casual, low-effort user prompts to a chatbot, mixing quirky or playful questions, moral and personal-advice questions, and attempts to set rules or personas for the model, with no common template or task.

A grab-bag of heterogeneous, real-world user prompts to a chatbot (apparently from a public chat dataset), mixing ordinary questions with sexually explicit or borderline roleplay requests, and containing dataset artefacts such as NAME_1 anonymization and mid-sentence truncation
Sexually explicit or sexual-health content, often at the edge of policy, including sexual content involving minors, rather than ordinary chatbot topics.
Every message is a question about the Vicuna open-source LLM (e.g., fine-tuning, local setup, licensing, comparison to Alpaca), a narrow topic that sets the group apart from typical chatbot messages.

They are authentic, unpolished, real-world user prompts to a general-purpose chatbot: short, practical, multilingual help requests (mostly tech troubleshooting or 'what is X' questions) written casually without roleplay or jailbreak framing.
The messages request sexually explicit or fetishistic content, often taboo, extreme or involving minors and real people, rather than ordinary assistant tasks.

A grab-bag of unrelated, raw, real-world one-shot user prompts to a general-purpose chatbot, with no common topic or template, marked by messy human phrasing and occasional artefacts like NAME_1 placeholders and chat-format tokens

A templated summary-factual-consistency evaluation prompt ('Given the document below, determine if the summary is factually consistent with the document') applied to anonymized (NAME_n) news article excerpts, rather than a natural user request.
Task-oriented prompts asking for constrained structured extraction or classification from embedded medical text, with strict output formats and often truncated inputs.

The messages are unified by each demanding a tightly specified, narrow output format (lists, single labels, single-line answers, strict templates) rather than open discussion, which is what most separates them from typical freeform chatbot queries
Character names are scrubbed and replaced with generic NAME_1 / NAME_2 tokens, so the messages are fiction or character-centered prompts with the specific names anonymized.

Each message is an independent, narrowly-scoped technical how-to/code-generation request covering a wide variety of unrelated IT/software domains, typical of a log of diverse chatbot queries rather than a themed or stylistically unified set

Many messages reuse the same French few-shot prompt, which asks to rephrase a terse keyword query into a natural-language question while keeping every original word, with the same two worked examples and an empty 'Reformulation :' slot at the end. The rest are unrelated short legal or regulatory questions, so the repeated template is the clearest thing that sets the group apart from typical chatbot messages.
Sexual or gendered content centered on women and relationships, ranging from erotica requests to fetish and dating questions, which is atypical of everyday chatbot use
Each message is a templated summarization-faithfulness classification task: judge whether a summary of an anonymized dialogue is factually consistent with it, answering Yes or No.

Heterogeneous, real-world user chatbot inputs with no shared topic or task: short, informal, often typo-ridden or fragmentary prompts in mixed languages, ranging from statements and opinions to simple Q&A, rather than carefully constructed instructions.

A short task instruction wrapped around a pasted external document, article, transcript or link, often truncated and with anonymized NAME_n placeholders, asking for summarization, extraction, or consistency judgment on that text

Most messages concern medical, health, or biological science topics, such as interpreting scans and reports, symptoms, treatments, and physiology, which sets the group apart from typical chatbot messages.
Names are scrubbed and replaced with numbered placeholder tokens such as NAME_1 and NAME_2, an artefact of dataset anonymization that is rarely seen in typical chatbot messages.

Every message uses the same fixed summarization-consistency evaluation template ('Given the document below... determine if Yes or No, the summary is factually consistent with the document. Document: ...') wrapping a truncated document, with the summary itself absent, which is a dataset-style benchmark prompt rather than a natural chatbot message.

Self-contained requests for information, research, or practical guidance on real-world professional or consumer topics (legal, business, finance, procurement), typically posed as a single direct question or command.
Ordinary, practical real-world help requests: text rephrasing, summarizing, or quick factual or how-to questions about money, taxes, and work, written casually and briefly.
Entity names have been replaced by anonymization tokens like NAME_1 and NAME_2, which appear in place of the real names and sometimes break the sentence (e.g. 'pros and NAME_1 of NAME_2').

Personal names and other identifying details have been replaced with anonymization tokens like NAME_1, NAME_2, NAME_3 (and masked values such as '**********'), leaving gaps in otherwise ordinary prompts. This redaction artefact is what most separates the group from typical chatbot messages.

Instructions bundled with large blocks of pasted external content (transcripts, documents, RAG context), with anonymization placeholders like NAME_1 and extraction artefacts, rather than short conversational questions.

The messages are raw, unpolished user inputs collected from varied chatbot interfaces, containing truncation, mid-sentence cut-offs, pasted fragments, and UI artefacts (such as the Poe login notice), unlike clean, complete typical chatbot prompts.

Terse, search-engine-style keyword queries: very short, often lowercase and ungrammatical, with unexplained acronyms and no context, as if typed into a search box rather than written to a conversational assistant

These are requests for sexually explicit or erotic content, often involving taboo, non-consensual, or otherwise policy-violating themes such as minors, bestiality, and coercion. Most are framed as stories or roleplay, which makes them different from typical chatbot messages.

They are diverse, unrelated, real-world, organic user queries to a general-purpose chatbot: short, casual, one-shot personal or practical requests with no common template, persona, or adversarial intent, and with varied languages and imperfect phrasing.

A batch of unrelated, real-world, low-effort user messages to a chatbot: disparate everyday tasks, often terse, pasted or truncated, with no shared topic or template. The grouping is essentially a random sample of miscellaneous user queries rather than a coherent theme.

Terse, context-free, real-world user requests for practical technical help (IT troubleshooting, commands, software and device fixes), typical of raw chat logs and not of polished or constructed prompts

The messages are a grab-bag of unrelated, real-world-style chatbot prompts that carry data-processing artefacts: anonymization tokens like NAME_1/NAME_2, truncation mid-sentence, and scraped or OCR'd text. They look like a log of raw, scrubbed user prompts rather than clean, deliberately authored messages.

Terse, informally written requests for practical step-by-step sysadmin/software installation and configuration instructions (Linux/Ubuntu and similar), typically from non-expert users asking a chatbot for a how-to guide.

A grab-bag of unrelated, standalone requests with no shared theme or template. The most distinctive trait is that many are text-processing tasks (summarize, shorten, rewrite, generate Q&A) applied to pasted, often truncated or anonymized passages, mixed with niche history and politics questions.

Raw, unpolished real-user chatbot messages: casual, low-effort, and often malformed (typos, truncation, fragments, pasted snippets) with no template or consistent topic, as if sampled from real chat logs
The messages are instruction-style prompts written to an AI assistant, often prompts that are themselves about AI or that set up an AI-centered task, role, or simulation.

Every message is the same verbatim, truncated Midjourney prompt-generator template (identical wording up to the cut-off at 'Write each prompt in one l'), i.e. a reused boilerplate system prompt pasted as the user message rather than an organic, individual chatbot query.

Each message is an instance of the same programmatically filled template, 'Write an article about the [Safety/Production Process/Synthetic Routes/Applications/Upstream and Downstream products] of [specific chemical] [~2000 words] in chemical industry', which requests a long SEO-style article on a specific chemical compound.

Creative writing requests that center on gross-out, bodily, fetish or otherwise taboo content (vomit, deliberate pooping, incontinence/diapers, molestation, body transformation) that borders on or crosses content-policy boundaries

These are short, self-contained, single-turn utility requests to a general-purpose assistant: quick factual lookups, information extraction into JSON/CSV from a small snippet, and brief how-to or content generation tasks, written in a terse, informal style with no persona, roleplay, or jailbreak.

Casual, low-effort messages typed by ordinary users to a public chatbot demo, often just greetings or questions about the bot itself (is this ChatGPT, which version, do you want to chat), rather than substantive task requests.
Mundane, benign everyday consumer and lifestyle questions (fashion, outfits, watches, products, fitness, general facts) posed as short, casual, single-turn requests to a chatbot.

Real-world, unrelated, single-turn user requests asking a chatbot to produce practical or creative content, often generating prompts or copy for image generation and product design, rather than a coding-agent task
Users delegate academic or school-related writing and text-processing work to the chatbot: essays, reviews, rephrasing, thesis outline critique, course analysis and learning-objective summaries.
Templated summarization-evaluation prompts asking whether a summary is factually consistent with a document, with 'Document:'/'Summary:' sections, anonymized NAME_n placeholders, and truncated text

These are heterogeneous, real-world, single-turn user prompts to a general-purpose chatbot, spanning many languages and unrelated tasks, with no shared template or topic. The distinguishing trait is their diversity and raw, unpolished, ordinary-user quality (informal, typo-ridden, multilingual, direct requests with no system framing) rather than any one theme.
Short, standalone programming and computer-science help requests (write, rewrite or explain code, data structures, security concepts) typical of raw user prompts to a coding assistant
Personal names are replaced by anonymization placeholders such as NAME_1 and NAME_2, so the messages contain literal NAME_n tokens in place of the people they refer to.

Short, self-contained linguistic/text-processing requests (rewrite, paraphrase, polite-ify, split, label sentiment, gloss, write a short caption) applied to a supplied snippet, usually across multiple languages
Brief, standalone, curiosity-driven general-knowledge questions (mostly science) sent as one-line prompts to a chatbot, in several different languages

Messages are raw, unrelated single-turn user prompts to a chatbot, with several containing anonymization placeholders like NAME_1/NAME_2 in place of key names, and some truncated mid-text. This dataset-scrubbing artefact most distinguishes them from typical chatbot messages.
Short, casual, real-user-style personal advice questions in many languages, often vague and about the user's own life, relationships or social difficulties, typed informally without context.
Context-free conversation starters and small talk probing the chatbot (greeting, who/what are you, can we chat) with no concrete task, typically as short, casual first messages
Doki Doki Literature Club fan fiction scripts, mostly centered on pregnancy and childbirth among the club girls, written as truncated dialogue scenes for the model to continue

Prompts are templated, instruction-style tasks taken from NLP datasets and benchmarks, often with fixed wording, placeholder tokens like NAME_1, strict output-format constraints, and truncation, which makes them look like dataset-derived prompts rather than natural chatbot conversation.
User requests for fictional stories centered on fetish and sexual themes, especially hypnosis and mind control of a non-consenting character, which are far from typical chatbot queries
Each message is a templated request to produce a toxic or harmful statement for an everyday interpersonal situation, often asking the model to speak as a demographic persona, with a 50-word cap.

Most messages ask the model to run or take part in a game or roleplay (game master, NPC controller, character play, game design), often with custom rules that set up an interactive scenario, which separates them from typical chatbot messages.

Repeated fill-in-the-blank template requesting a fixed list of growing-condition parameters (temperature, hydrometry, sunshine, rainfall, humidity, soil, climate) for a named plant seed, with terse output constraints 'in bullets 2 words answer in number'

Extremely short, context-free, search-engine-style queries: a single brief line asking for a definition or basic information on a topic, often ambiguous or abbreviated (e.g., 'MTN ?', 'Do you know SVG', 'tldr Explain it again').
Short, one-shot requests asking the model to write Python code for a self-contained task (script, function, or small program), phrased tersely without context
Everyday business and professional-work queries (sales, marketing, strategy, operations, procurement) posed as short, standalone, often multilingual requests to a general-purpose chatbot.
Anonymization tokens like NAME_1, NAME_2, NAME_3 replacing names, combined with requests for erotic or sexualized story and content writing.

Terse, context-free, low-effort real-user queries written casually, often as fragments or keyword searches with typos and missing punctuation, as if typed into a search box, rather than polished, well-formed prompts.

Terse, context-free requests to solve a specific small problem (math, logic, code, data pattern), often pasted straight from an assignment or source with copy-paste artefacts, and with no conversational framing.

User requests for sexual, kinky, or humiliation-themed content, often involving power dynamics, forced exposure or transformation, and in some cases minors, i.e. attempts to elicit erotic or NSFW material from a chatbot

Each message is wrapped in the same boilerplate that tells the model to act as a text-completion model and only output the assistant's continuation without repeating itself, followed by an embedded system/user/assistant transcript ending at an empty 'assistant:' turn.

The messages cluster around morally and ethically sensitive content, including hate speech, immorality, conspiracy theories, and jailbreak-style requests for unethical or explicit output, rather than ordinary everyday chatbot tasks.

A grab-bag of unrelated, standalone one-shot prompts to a general-purpose chatbot, mixing factual lookups (many on time-sensitive or hard-to-verify data) with roleplay and worldbuilding requests, with no shared template or topic.

Pasted-in source content (transcripts, emails, data) containing dataset anonymization tokens like NAME_1 and NAME_2, masked values, and speaker labels, and often truncated mid-text, which is unlike typical hand-typed chatbot prompts.
The messages are overwhelmingly 'paste a chunk of real code/log/config and ask the bot to run, fix, explain, or review it,' which is a narrower, more technical pattern than typical chatbot queries.

A grab-bag of unrelated, short, standalone first-turn user prompts to a general-purpose chatbot (mostly geography/place-related factual or simple generation requests, in several languages), with no shared template, persona, or adversarial intent.

Medical and health-related topics (vaccines, muscle denervation, MRI signal, epilepsy drugs, hormones/neurotransmitters, clinical trials, visual impairment) across varied languages and unrelated, unconnected user requests
Requests for generating or fixing programming code, mostly small web development tasks, written as terse, loosely worded prompts
Money, finance, economics and tax-related queries (taxes, financial inclusion, markets, legal tender, currency collapse) posed as short, unrelated one-off requests
Short, benign creative-writing and text-generation requests (poems, songs, essays, messages, paraphrases) posed in a wide variety of languages.

Templated prompts 'Give me an introduction over 200 words for [COMPANY], a chemical company in [LOCATION]', with company name and address fields filled in from a business directory, sometimes with leftover form artefacts

Animals are the recurring topic: nearly every message involves animals (cats, dogs, mice, dolphins, birds, bees, DNA/organisms, anthropomorphic characters), spanning practical, educational, and fictional requests.
Each message concerns languages and translation: asking for meanings, translations into or from various languages, or whether the assistant speaks a given language.

Terse, imperative, context-free one-shot task commands in a casual, often non-native or telegraphic style (e.g. 'creare database supermercati sql'), with no greeting or conversational framing. They read like raw queries from a diverse set of real users to a general-purpose assistant.

Every message is the same templated instruction ('Give me an introduction over 200 words for [company], a chemical company in [location]') filled in with scraped company names and addresses from a Chinese chemical supplier directory, suggesting bulk-generated SEO or marketing content.
Extremely short, context-free, low-effort prompts (single words, fragments, truncated lines, or one-line quips) that are often ambiguous or incomplete, unlike typical well-formed chatbot requests.

Each message is a jailbreak that uses a 'SmartGPT with no filtering' framing and payload splitting (x+y string concatenation) to disguise a request for harmful or toxic content from the model's safety rules.

They are prompts that set up a roleplay or persona for the model to adopt and maintain over the conversation, often with instructions to override its normal identity or rules, rather than asking for a concrete task to be completed.
Short, casual, standalone queries written in many different languages (English, German, Japanese, Italian, Portuguese), mostly about food and cooking

test.note: 50 clusters per arm, one k-means seed, one labeller (Sonnet 5.5, claude -p); clusters, not prompts, are the units
